key_insight: Greater adherence to the MIND diet was associated with lower subsequent epigenetic aging across three DNA methylation measures.
clinical_relevance: The findings support molecular aging markers for diet–aging research but do not establish that the MIND diet slows aging or improves clinical outcomes.
method: Linked 2013 dietary data with 2016 DNA methylation measures in 1,740 Health and Retirement Study participants.
Used adjusted models and targeted maximum likelihood estimation to assess associations.
Used causal forests with held-out and repeated-split evaluation to explore subgroup differences.
evidence_signal: Per 1-SD higher MIND score, PhenoAge acceleration was 0.4 years lower, GrimAge acceleration 0.3 years lower, and methylation Pace of Aging 0.0054 lower; all FDR q≤0.026, with no reproducible subgroup differences.
watch_item: This observational analysis cannot establish causality; residual confounding may remain despite adjustment and selection weighting.
paper_title: Concordance with the MIND diet is associated with lower subsequent epigenetic aging
